statement: A data analyst fits the line of best fit $y = 4.5x + 12$ to a set of data points. She then learns that every $x$-value was recorded $2$ units too small, so she adds $2$ to each $x$-value and leaves each $y$-value unchanged. Which equation is the line of best fit for the corrected data?

choices.misconception: I subtracted 2 from the y-intercept, as if moving the points 2 units right lowered the line by 2, but the drop is 2 times the slope.
I knew the intercept changes by 2 times the slope, but I added the 9 instead of subtracting it, which moves the line left instead of right.
I added the 2 to the slope, but sliding every point sideways moves the line without changing how steep it is.

hints: Does moving every point $2$ units right change how steep the line is?
The new line is the old line shifted $2$ units to the right. Replace $x$ with $x - 2$ in the old equation.
The corrected line is $y = 4.5(x - 2) + 12$. Expand it.

solutions.reliable: Adding $2$ to every $x$-value moves every data point $2$ units to the right, so the line of best fit moves $2$ units to the right with the same slope. Replacing $x$ with $x - 2$: $y = 4.5(x - 2) + 12 = 4.5x - 9 + 12 = 4.5x + 3$. Check: the old line passes through $(0, 12)$; that point moves to $(2, 12)$, and $4.5(2) + 3 = 12$.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
